- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.5) over recent days, model tends to under-forecast upward momentum; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% of recent mean.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and price is trending down, model often over-anticipates recovery; reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overshoot.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overreacts with excessive upward bias; apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 2–5% from forecast for next 3–5 days.
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.2–0.8) and price shows no clear trend, model often overfits short-term noise; use 3-day moving average to smooth forecast.
- Model tends to under-forecast mean reversion in high-sentiment periods; if sentiment >0.6 for 5+ days, add 0.5–1.5% upward bias to reflect potential continuation.
- In low-sentiment (≤0.2) periods, model often under-estimates downside risk; add 0.5–1.5% downward buffer to forecast if sentiment remains below 0.3 for 3+ days.
- Forecast horizon >14 days: model tends to lag in capturing sentiment-driven momentum; apply 1–2% lag correction (forecast = true - 1–2% of recent 7-day mean) if sentiment is trending.
- If sentiment history shows “reversal” (e.g., 0.8 → 0.2 → 0.8), model often misjudges turning point; delay forecast adjustment by 1–2 days until sentiment stabilizes.
